body:
OBJECTIVES
- Students express a fraction with denominator 10 as an equivalent fraction with denominator 100, and add two fractions with denominators 10 and 100 (4.NF.C.5).
- Students use decimal notation for fractions with denominators 10 or 100 and locate decimals on a number line (4.NF.C.6).
- Students compare two decimals to hundredths by reasoning about their size, record comparisons with >, = or <, and recognize that comparisons are valid only when the decimals refer to the same whole (4.NF.C.7).

MATERIALS
- Hundred grids (printed 10 by 10 squares) and colored pencils
- Play money: dollars, dimes and pennies
- A large number line from 0 to 2 marked in tenths
- A place value chart with ones, tenths and hundredths

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Fractions in Disguise. Shade hundred grids to show 3/10 and 30/100 and see they are the same area. Lesson: Tenths and Hundredths.
Day 2: Money mini-lesson: build amounts with dimes and pennies and write them as fractions and decimals. Add tenths and hundredths with the grid.
Day 3: Number line mini-lesson: place decimals between 0 and 2 on a class number line. Start Decimals on the Number Line.
Day 4: Finish Decimals on the Number Line. Discuss Jamal's mistake: write each decimal in hundredths before comparing.
Day 5: Assessment: Decimal Check.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: keep the hundred grid and the place value chart available; compare decimals by shading both on grids.
- Support: use money for every problem first (0.4 is 4 dimes, 0.38 is 3 dimes and 8 pennies).
- Stretch: place 0.125? No: keep to hundredths, and instead have students find three decimals between 0.4 and 0.5 and explain how they know.
- Multilingual learners: say decimals aloud in two ways ("zero point four five" and "forty-five hundredths") and connect each to the grid. Many countries use a comma as the decimal mark; welcome that knowledge and show both.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
We are learning about decimals, which are fractions with denominators of 10 and 100. Money is a great way to practice: a dime is one tenth of a dollar ($0.10) and a penny is one hundredth ($0.01). At the store or with coins at home, ask your child to show amounts like $0.35 with dimes and pennies, or to tell which price is greater: $0.40 or $0.38.
title: Teacher guide: Decimals: Tenths and Hundredths
